title: CEO Narcissism and Corporate Risk-Taking: The Contingent Moderating Role of Governance Mechanisms Across Developed and Emerging Markets
content: This study examines whether observed CEO narcissism is associated with corporate strategic risk-taking, and whether governance mechanisms attenuate this association differently across developed and emerging markets. To address the theoretical fragmentation surrounding these relationships, we develop the Institutional-Contingent Narcissistic Risk-Governance (ICNRG) framework, which integrates Upper Echelons Theory, Agency Theory, Institutional Theory, and — as a central pillar — the theory of Managerial Discretion. Perceptual data from 452 financial analysts, institutional investors, and fund managers across 14 countries (7 developed, 7 emerging) were analysed using hierarchical moderated regression with heteroskedasticity-robust HC3 standard errors and multi-group structural analyses. Results indicate that CEO narcissism, as observed by external market participants, is positively associated with corporate risk-taking. Governance quality is negatively related to risk in both markets, but a Chow test of coefficient equality (F = 23.30, p < .001) confirms that the strength of these associations differs sharply across institutional contexts: the governance–risk association is markedly stronger in emerging markets than in developed markets. A CFA marker-variable procedure and a comprehensive measurement-model assessment suggest that common method bias does not meaningfully inflate the observed associations. We frame these findings as an advance — rather than a resolution — of the debate on how institutions shape the boundary conditions of executive personality effects. The study offers implications for corporate governance policy in institutional-void contexts and outlines a longitudinal agenda for causal identification.
